solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Have sex with Bobby – at a distance

blocks.note: a bobby is a British police officer, slang cop
far off, away

explanation.surface: Someone propositions a policeman, but only from a safe distance.
explanation.walkthrough: A bobby is the old British nickname for a police officer, after Sir Robert Peel. To cop off is British slang for pulling someone.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, copping off with someone means getting together with them sexually, often after a night out.

clue.text: Violet chewed cud in London, say – mayoral obligation?

indicators.note: food that has been chewed is mashed about, so these letters get mangled into a new order
one thing being in another means it sits inside it, wrapped round

blocks.note: the first two letters of the name, its usual pet form
the three letters of the word, to be rearranged
London is an example of a city, signalled by 'say'

explanation.surface: A girl called Violet chomps on cud in London, oddly framed as a duty for the mayor.
explanation.walkthrough: The cow image of chewing cud is a red herring; 'chewed' only scrambles the word, and 'say' warns that London is just an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A mayor carries out public responsibilities for the town, which are precisely what citizens call civic duties; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Prince affectedly "creative":  badly managed by Starmer?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the noun: the Labour party

blocks.note: P is the standard abbreviation for prince
arty means pretentiously artistic

explanation.surface: A satirical jab: a pretentious prince, and a Labour leader who runs things poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: Arty is the mocking word for showily creative. Keir Starmer led the Labour Party, which Private Eye suggests he runs badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Starmer leads a political organisation, the Labour group, so the thing he manages badly is his own political grouping.

clue.text: Disapprove of what Brenda has to have for ceremonial occasions (with new top)

indicators.note: a new top means the first letter is swapped out for a different one

blocks.clueFragment: what Brenda has to have for ceremonial occasions
blocks.note: Brenda is Private Eye's name for the late Queen, who wore her crown at state events

explanation.surface: The Queen must don her regalia for state ceremonies, and someone disapproves.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II. CROWN ON gets a new first letter, F, which the clue leaves to the definition and crossers.
explanation.definitionFit: To frown on something is an idiom for regarding it with disapproval, as if scowling at it.

clue.text: Eccentric earl needs adjustable legging elasticated tops for proper piss?

indicators.note: something eccentric is off-centre and odd, so the letters are set out of their usual order
the top of a word is its first letter, so only the leading letters are kept

blocks.note: the four letters rearranged
the initial letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: An odd aristocrat in stretchy leggings is headed for a serious drinking session.
explanation.walkthrough: Piss is British slang for beer, and real ale is traditional cask-conditioned British beer, so 'proper piss' is a cheeky definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Real ale is authentic cask beer as opposed to fizzy keg lager, so it is genuine, proper drink in rude slang.

clue.text: Stretch old underwear it's said

indicators.note: what is said is heard rather than read, so the sound counts and not the spelling

blocks.note: ex means former, and pants are British underpants

explanation.surface: Old underwear that has been stretched out of shape, as people complain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch' looks like a verb about the elastic; it is a noun. In British English pants are underpants, not trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: An expanse is a wide continuous area, a stretch of land or sea, so the noun sense matches.

clue.text: Family blood type acceptable? Refuse to go into it

blocks.note: a litter is a family of young animals born together
B is one of the ABO blood groups
in means fashionable, acceptable

explanation.surface: A family question about blood types, and someone refusing to go along with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as the verb to decline; it is the noun meaning rubbish, stressed on the first syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: A litter bin is a public receptacle where rubbish is thrown, so waste goes into it.

clue.text: see 22ac.
Arrangement with bank that should have you on your feet

definitions.text: that should have you on your feet

blocks.note: first meaning: an instruction to a bank to pay a fixed sum regularly

blocks.clueFragment: that should have you on your feet
blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: a command telling you to rise

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is the phrase taken literally: an order to stand.
explanation.definitionFit: British banks offer a regular automatic payment instruction under this name, and literally a command to be upright fits too.

clue.text: On top, firm, coming to a violent end – that should keep you warm

indicators.note: an end of a word is its final letter, so just that one is kept

blocks.note: over means above, on top
Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
taken as written
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dominant company meets a violent end, with a note about keeping warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A violent end' splits into A plus the last letter of violent; it is not a description of the firm's fate.
explanation.definitionFit: An overcoat is a heavy outer garment worn in cold weather for warmth, so the descriptive phrase fits.

clue.text: "State ain't budging!" – Sheen

indicators.note: budging means shifting position, so the letters move about

blocks.note: PA is the abbreviation for Pennsylvania, a US state
the four letters, ignoring the apostrophe, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A defiant state government refuses to move, quoted alongside the actor Sheen.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheen looks like Martin or Charlie Sheen the actors; it is the definition. 'Ain't budging' cleverly turns a refusal to move into a movement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A patina is the glossy surface film that develops on wood or bronze with age, a gentle lustre.

clue.text: Feeling pain from a chain applied to tip of willy

indicators.note: a tip is an extremity, here the final letter of the word

blocks.note: taken as written
ch is the abbreviation for chain, an old unit of length
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A painful-sounding scene of a chain attached somewhere delicate.
explanation.walkthrough: A chain is a surveying length of 22 yards, abbreviated ch. Willy is British slang for penis.
explanation.definitionFit: Achy describes a body suffering dull continuous soreness, the adjective for being in mild pain.

clue.text: Working to switch round balls, nothing fancy

indicators.note: switching something round turns it to face the other way

blocks.note: a machine that is working is on
balls is British slang for rubbish talk

explanation.surface: Someone's job involves turning balls round, plainly and without frills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is the British exclamation for nonsense, as in 'what a load of balls'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something no-nonsense is simple, practical and businesslike, with no frills or decoration.

clue.text: Managed to get into quite an awful, unwelcome end to foreign holiday?

indicators.note: something awful is in a terrible state, so the letters are thrown into disorder
getting into something means going inside it

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
the letters of the two words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone manages to have a dreadful finish to a trip abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Jumbled QUITE AN becomes QUATINE, which then takes RAN inside it. Covid-era travellers returning home often had to isolate on arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: Quarantine is enforced isolation, which during the pandemic often greeted travellers coming back from overseas trips.

clue.text: Call on crook to guarantee funds won't be misused

blocks.note: to ring is to phone, to call
a fence is a criminal who deals in stolen goods

explanation.surface: Phoning a criminal to make sure money stays safe, an ironic plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call on' suggests visiting; 'on' just places one piece after the other in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring-fence money is to protect it so it can only be spent on a designated purpose.

clue.text: Bare skin enthusiast

blocks.note: first meaning: naked skin
second meaning: a keen fan, as in a film devotee

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it suggests a naturist; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means naked skin in the phrase 'in the buff' and also a knowledgeable fan of a hobby.

clue.text: Country confiscating tabloid gets bouquet

indicators.note: confiscating something means seizing and holding it, so one piece takes another inside

blocks.note: a European country
a rag is a disparaging word for a low-quality newspaper

explanation.surface: A government seizes a scandal sheet and gets flowers in return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bouquet' wants to mean flowers; here it is the wine-taster's word for smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Bouquet is the characteristic aroma of a wine, a synonym for a pleasant scent or perfume.

clue.text: Cold? No turning blue!

indicators.note: turning round makes something face back the way it came

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
nay is an old word for no

explanation.surface: Someone asks if you are cold and warns you are not turning blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Turning blue from cold is the natural picture, but 'turning' reverses the word for no.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyan is a greenish shade of blue, one of the printing primary colours.

clue.text: Germaine screwed around with short lieutenant of the colonel's command

indicators.note: being screwed around means being messed about, so the letters are disordered

blocks.note: the name taken as written
Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: Gossip that Germaine had a fling with an army officer serving under the colonel.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of GERMAINE plus LT is rearranged. Private Eye readers will think of Germaine Greer.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonel commands a regiment, so anything belonging to that unit is described with this adjective.

clue.text: Take a lecherous look back at Dicky and give a faultless recitation

indicators.note: going back means running in the opposite direction

blocks.note: to leer is to look with sexual intent
dicky is British slang for unwell or faulty, as is off

explanation.surface: Someone ogles a man called Dicky and then recites something perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a name; it is the British adjective for unreliable or poorly, as in a dicky heart.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel off a list is to recite it rapidly and fluently without hesitation or error.

clue.text: Jaws operator responsible for artist and Brenda getting together

blocks.note: Edvard Munch, the Norwegian painter of The Scream
Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen, ER

explanation.surface: The film-maker behind Jaws arranged for a painter and the Queen to meet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jaws operator' suggests Spielberg; it means someone working their jaws. ER is Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who munches chews steadily, so they are literally operating their jaws while eating.

clue.text: Hot air associated with club's kitchen aid

blocks.note: waffle is empty, long-winded talk
an iron is a type of golf club

explanation.surface: A club bore's endless talk is somehow linked to a gadget for the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' suggests a society; here it is a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: A waffle iron is a hinged griddle used for cooking batter, a piece of kitchen equipment.

clue.text: London borough chief ignored Archer's release

indicators.note: the chief letter is the first one, and ignoring it leaves it out

blocks.note: Harrow is a borough in north-west London

explanation.surface: A London council leader is overlooked while Jeffrey Archer gets out of prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Archer suggests the novelist Jeffrey Archer, jailed for perjury; here it is anyone with a bow.
explanation.definitionFit: An archer shoots by letting go of the bowstring, and what flies off is the projectile.

clue.text: (& 7dn.) What an actor learns after having an erection: "Too bad"

indicators.note: coming after something means following it, so the piece named second here goes first in the answer

blocks.note: rude slang for being aroused
an actor memorises the words of a part, which are spoken one row of script at a time

explanation.surface: A smutty theatrical anecdote: an actor learning a script while aroused, met with sympathy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts one piece behind the other, so the second piece comes first. Hard lines is a British expression of commiseration.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard lines is a dated British exclamation of sympathy meaning bad luck, an idiom equivalent to 'tough'.

clue.text: Labour leader at centre of own split

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is kept
something at the centre of another sits inside it

blocks.note: to own is to have
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: The Labour leader is at the heart of a split in his own party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' looks like Starmer; it is the first letter of Labour. 'Own split' reads as a noun phrase but the verb is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To halve something is to divide it into two equal parts, a synonym for the verb split.

clue.text: Immediately in favour of not getting pissed

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and a drunk staggers out of order

blocks.note: pro means for, in favour of
the three letters, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone declares they are all for staying sober, right now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not getting pissed' reads as a vow of sobriety, but the drunk word scrambles 'not'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pronto is informal for right away, borrowed from Spanish and Italian words for quick or ready.

clue.text: Former nickname of Henry, the TV presenter, a Covid-spreader?

blocks.note: ex means former
Hal is a pet form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal
Ant McPartlin of the British presenting duo Ant and Dec

explanation.surface: An old nickname for Henry, a TV host, and the suggestion he spread Covid.
explanation.walkthrough: Ant and Dec are a hugely popular British TV presenting pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Covid spreads through breath, so anyone or anything that breathes out could be called an exhalant, with a question mark for the stretch.

clue.text: Wholesome female having been given one: "Not a thing"

blocks.note: sweet can mean wholesome and pleasant
F is the abbreviation for female
a means one

explanation.surface: A wholesome woman is handed something and says it is nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet FA, short for 'sweet Fanny Adams' (or a ruder phrase), is British slang for nothing; 'given one' also hints at something ruder.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet FA is a British euphemistic expression meaning absolutely nothing, the same as zilch.

clue.text: The country's broadcast smear

indicators.note: what is broadcast is heard over the air, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: grease is something smeared on

explanation.surface: A national broadcaster runs a smear campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast smear' reads as a media attack; 'smear' is the stuff, not the slander.
explanation.definitionFit: Greece is a nation in south-east Europe, so 'the country' names it generically.
